articles.title: Unlearned lessons
articles.content: THEtalksbetween the government and the opposition were doomed from the outset, even though the fact that the two sides sat face to face at the negotiating table was a positive sign. The meeting took place under the shadow of the PTI’s threatenedlong marchto Islamabad, while the government brandished the option of governor’s rule in KP. The tension was palpable. The capital was sealed off with containers and the highways were blocked. Days before the talks, the military leadership warned against any repeat of a May 9-like situation — a clear message to the opposition not to cross the red line. Some opposition leaders, for their part, wanted a negotiated deal to bring down the political temperature. The prolonged discussions suggested a measure of seriousness on both sides, but mutual distrust and brinkmanship blocked any breakthrough. The two sides gave contrary accounts of why the talks collapsed after a marathon sitting. The governmentcontendedthat the opposition backed out after agreeing to a final draft; the other side denied this, saying the differences were too wide to bridge. That so-called final draft is not in the public domain, but two major points of difference appear to have defeated the agreement. The PTI insisted on a meeting with Imran Khan, while the government wanted the KP provincial government to give unqualified support to the counterterrorism operation being carried out by the security forces. While conceding to the opposition’s demand that the former prime minister be allowed to meet his family and his lawyers, as ordered by the Islamabad High Court, and agreeing to implement the Supreme Courtorderto arrange his medical treatment, the government was not prepared to let PTI leaders meet and consult him before finalising the agreement — a condition it found unacceptable. The prevailing political instability has provided greater space to the militants. The real cause of the stalemate, however, was the issue of provincial government support, and taking ownership of a planned counterterrorism military operation in five southern districts, including the merged Fata regions. For the provincial government this was an extremely tricky matter: it had strongly opposed any kinetic operation involving the displacement of the population, and the bitter memories of earlier operations had created intense public opposition to any such action. A multiparty meeting called by the provincial government early this year — whose participants included provincial legislators belonging to PML-N, PPP and ANP — had unanimously opposed any large-scale military operation. Considering this, it was hard for the PTI to take ownership of a highly unpopular action. It may be true that the PTI has no clarity over how to combat the menace of terrorism that has swept a large part of the province. Its inaction, often seen as capitulation, has added to the problem. The ill-equipped police and Counter Terrorism Department have been a major target of militants, resulting in a virtual collapse of the administration in the troubled districts. That inaction could also be attributed to the ongoing confrontation between the PTI and the establishment-backed federal government. Then there is the question of whether we have a coherent, overarching national security policy and counterterrorism strategy to deal with this existential threat. There has rarely been any debate in parliament on internal security policy. It is all left to the security establishment, with hardly any policy input from the civilian leadership. KP has witnessed a strong resurgence of militancy over the last five years, which has claimed the lives of thousands of civilians and security personnel. Last year saw the highest number of terrorist attacks in the province since 2013, despite claims of successful intelligence operations that killed hundreds of terrorists. The prevailing political instability has provided greater space to the militants, who are now better equipped and better organised, and who have extended their activities to other parts of the province. Pakistan has blamed Afghanistan’s Taliban regime for providing sanctuaries and aiding the TTP, and each major terrorist attack is now answered by Pakistani strikes across the border. The closure of the border and of trade between the two countries over the past year has directly affected the local population and added to the tension between Peshawar and Islamabad. There is a serious disconnect in the policy the establishment pursues in dealing with terrorism, and the government needs to address those concerns. There are no two views about the imperatives of a national security policy, but there is also a need to bring all stakeholders on board for an overarching policy that should not rest entirely on kinetic operations. It is important to address the social and economic issues in order to win public support in the affected areas. The widening trust gap between the state and the people, and the politics of confrontation, are the biggest hurdles in combating terrorism. With little hope of the two sides returning to the negotiating table, the confrontation has now escalated: the PTI has begun its protest march from the southern KP districts. It is apparent that the PTI has changed its strategy of marching directly on Islamabad. Instead, the party now plans to mobilise its supporters in the province and camp close to the capital rather than march into the city. It is the first instance of a chief executive leading a protest that paralyses his own province. Meanwhile, the federal government is considering removing the PTI government and imposing a state of emergency or governor’s rule in the province. That would be an extremely dangerous move in a province already facing terrorist attacks, rising nationalism and tension on its border. Any such move by a state already fighting a separatist movement in Balochistan and a revolt-like situation in Azad Kashmir would be disastrous. The province is sitting on a powder keg, and the removal from power of an elected government that enjoys an overwhelming majority in the provincial assembly and broad popular support could ignite it in a way the state would struggle to extinguish. We never learn lessons from our own history, and make the same mistake again and again and expect different results.
articles.author: Zahid Hussain

articles.title: Dual citizen? Debarred
articles.content: IT was a Friday afternoon in May 2019. State Bank of Pakistan Governor Tariq Bajwa was in Islamabad with the IMF mission, flanked by his technical team I led. Unbeknownst to him, his successor was already in the country. By evening, Bajwa had resigned. The finance secretary at the time told me a new governor would be appointed by nightfall: Reza Baqir, the IMF’s resident representative in Egypt, already in town and ready to assume charge. The notification followed the next day, a Saturday. Within 24 hours, over a weekend, a serving IMF official had been installed at the helm of the central bank, as abruptly as Bajwa’s own 2017 appointment had followed a rupee devaluation. Opacity is not the only problem; law compounds it. The 2022 amendments to the SBP Act, while granting welcome operational autonomy, also imposed restrictions found nowhere in the IMF’s own safeguards assessment: an outright bar on dual nationals, and a requirement that a candidate completes a full five-year term before turning 65. Together, these eliminate precisely the cohort best placed to lead the central bank, favouring insiders over competence. Contrast this with how Britain appoints the governor of the Bank of England: open international advertisement, a shortlist, ministerial interviews, and months of public notice before the transition begins. That is the process that produced Andrew Bailey to succeed Mark Carney in March 2020. In Pakistan, favoured candidates are installed within a day, while everyone else waits months, even years, for a vacancy the law says must be filled within 30 days. Mark Carney’s trajectory sharpens the point further. A Canadian citizen who also held Irish citizenship through family ancestry, he was appointed governor of the Bank of England in Nov 2012, and ran UK monetary policy and financial stability for nearly seven years, through the 2016 Brexit shock. In 2018, while still governor, he acquired British citizenship too, holding three nationalities as custodian of Britain’s currency, with no credible case that he favoured Canadian or Irish interests over British ones. Central banking is one of the few institutions where competence, not compliance, should be the only test. Stanley Fischer, author of three of the most influential economics textbooks, and former first deputy managing director of the IMF, served as vice chair of the US Federal Reserve from 2014 to 2017, while holding two citizenships, from age 70 to 74. More recently, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand appointed Dr Anna Breman, a Swedish national, as its first female governor. Dr Breman’s appointment in Aug 2025 followed a rigorous recruitment process, that even involved a global executive search firm. Baqir is the more contested recent case, but the criticism was never really about a passport; it was that an IMF insider negotiating a Pakistani programme sat ‘on both sides of the table’, a concern about institutional capture, not nationality. The consequences have been predictable. The governor’s post fell vacant in May 2022 and took over three months to fill, breaching the SBP Act’s 30-day requirement; a deputy governor’s post vacant since Nov 2024 was filled only in Aug 2026. Leadership has increasingly gone to candidates with modest qualifications, and qualified economists are either sidelined or leaving the SBP, a brain drain that is entirely self-inflicted. Brain drain is estimated to cost Pakistan roughly $4.2 billion annually. Pakistan’s economy, sustained by remittances, external borrowing, real estate speculation, and import-led consumption rather than exports, demands sophisticated leadership, not a bureaucratic placeholder chosen for compliance. Article 63(1)(c) bars dual nationals from parliament since an elected official answers to voters as the sole political principal, and a second citizenship competes with that loyalty. A central bank governor is not elected, but appointed, and constrained by statute, audit, parliamentary review, and a monetary policy committee, an accountability built on expertise, not a mandate. That is why dual nationality has long been lawful for the wider civil service, precisely because competence, not electoral legitimacy, is what those roles select for. A 2025 Senate report counted roughly 2,365 civil servants or their spouses holding dual nationality under that lawful regime. Extending the Article 63 logic to appointed posts applies a rule built for one office to a fundamentally different one. The government’s 2026 policy, read past the headline, already leans this way: the Civil Servants (Disclosure and Regulation of Foreign Nationality) Rules require employees to disclose foreign citizenship annually, treating concealment, not citizenship itself, as misconduct. It is a disclosure regime, not a blanket bar. A second passport is often acquired for reasons of economics and convenience, educating children, or freedom to travel, not disloyalty. The genuine concerns — divided loyalty, foreign leverage, capture by a foreign employer — are real, and better addressed by targeted tools than a passport count: disclosure of foreign assets, recusal where a conflict is shown, and cooling-off periods after work for a foreign government or an institution like the IMF. The US Federal Reserve applies this to its officials. It also catches the single-passport holder who has taken money from a foreign government, someone a citizenship test would wave through. Pakistan need not start from scratch. In 2022, the prime minister notified the ISI as the Special Vetting Agency for public office holders. The mechanism only needs streamlining to run on specific safeguards, not opaque “cleared” or “not cleared” verdicts that strip the federal government’s own statutory appointment authority. It is time to remove the dual-nationality bar and age restrictions on appointments to the governor, deputy governor, and Monetary Policy Committee positions. Central banking is one of the few institutions where competence, not compliance, should be the only test. The question worth asking of any candidate is not how many passports are in their drawer, but whether their record and enforceable safeguards assure they will act in the country’s interest. A passport count answers none of that. Performance, integrity, and disclosure do. The writer is the author of The Shady Economics of International Aid, and holds a PhD in economics from the University of Cambridge. He has served as chief economist of the State Bank and senior advisor to the IMF.
articles.author: Saeed Ahmed

articles.title: Homes for humans
articles.content: THE last few weeks brought bad news for urban settlements across the globe. Bangkok and other parts of Thailand experienced torrential rains and urban flooding that paralysed life. Thousands of hapless residents were hastily evacuated to safer locations. For many, this catastrophe meant losing their homes. Butwal and Kathmandu in Nepal were severely flooded; many people were swept away. Meanwhile, several cities and settlements also faced conflict-related harm as various weapons caused unprecedented disruptions to daily life. The economic toll is immense. The extraordinary rise in fuel prices has made life miserable for ordinary people. Against this backdrop, with war clouds continuing to darken many parts of the Middle East and beyond, World Habitat Day was recently marked, inviting all to address the emerging challenges to settlements and civilisation. One goal of this day is to review problems such as shelter and amenities. This year, climate events — long heatwaves, heavy rains in the north, and negligible rainfall in Karachi — make it difficult to recharge peri-urban aquifers. Drought-like conditions signal tough times for agriculture and livestock breeders. Housing issues have multiplied due to terrorism in KP and Balochistan. People from terrorism-affected districts are migrating to safer areas, creating shelter challenges in urban centres. Therefore, housing strategies for displaced populations are vital, as are sustained scientific responses to all these issues. Urban planning is a process. It entails tangible and intangible attributes such as access to education and livelihood, safety, infrastructure, and more. Constructing a few units alone hardly serves the purpose. Authorities can make a difference by adopting a catalytic approach. The primary element is land. Common problems include physical damage from inundation, a high water table, changing topography, rising vulnerability, and ownership or occupancy disputes. Whether it is Punjab or Swat, the problems are the same; they only vary in intensity. This situation demands an urgent policy response. A district-level land-use plan is the priority. This task needs input from provincial revenue, forest, and planning and development departments. The flooding profile, meteorological information, and broader climatic details should form the baseline of this endeavour. Urban planning involves tangible and intangible attributes. The scale of the housing need is another major factor. Provincial governments, which are now responsible for tackling the challenge, have yet to come up with a holistic strategy to house the shelterless as well as those living in inhuman situations. It is also evident that the government cannot build homes for such a vast number of affected people. In any case, housing cannot be directly subsidised because of the enormous cost and resource intensity. However, the government can help create enabling options for people to build their own houses and other facilities through various means. Upgrading brick kilns and mud block manufacturing facilities, along with setting up building material shops, can be an intervention with far-reaching impact. Ordinary folk have social and economic ties with commercial enterprises, which generate informal mechanisms for getting technical advice and credit. Relevant government departments can facilitate skill upgradation for artisans such as masons, carpenters, and earth workers, while technical and vocational authorities responsible for building a network of training centres in the provinces must be approached to devise appropriate skill-enhancement programmes. Additionally, university departments are providing expert assistance to assess solutions and support improvements to available options. Local and national NGOs have done a lot for social mobilisation, but this still needs to be scaled up so that inputs reach communities and empower them. Other bodies can also contribute by examining niche areas and sectors. The country’s ongoing economic crisis could benefit from housing development initiatives, which promise transformative outcomes. One can draw inspiration from ‘the New Deal’ programmes launched by the US government during the Great Depression in the 1930s. By enhancing social safety nets, creating purposeful employment opportunities, and building the labour force’s capacity, America lifted itself out of an economic and social abyss. If we use housing development as a starting point and adopt a similar approach, we can secure the same benefits for our beleaguered millions. The writer is an academic and researcher in Karachi.
articles.author: Dr Noman Ahmed

articles.title: Before the flood
articles.content: WHETHER or not the bizarre flydubai caper last week was a false-flag operation, Benjamin Netanyahu certainly seemed well-prepared to milk the drama for every possible drop of propaganda. Barely credible tales of derring-do were widely broadcast soon after the incident. Various discrepancies in the official narrative and supplementary visual components have attracted widespread scepticism. But just days after warning of unspecified attacks in the run-up to the Oct 27 elections, the Israeli PM desperately needed a distraction. Seemingly irrefutable evidence has been piling up that he was personally warned about a possibly unprecedented Hamas action just days before the Oct 7 Gaza breakout three years ago. The information came from two of Israel’s leading allies in the Arab world: the UAE and Egypt. The external warnings followed efforts by Hamas itself, during indirect discussions between the two sides about easing the Gaza blockade and releasing Palestinian prisoners, to inform the Israeli authorities about impending violence if the talks failed. Sufian Abu Zaida, reportedly a senior Fatah official picked by Israel as a mediator, who was trusted by both Hamas and Israel’s domestic security agency Shin Bet, relayed Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar’s threat of an imminent ‘earthquake’ to his Israeli interlocutors, as well as to Palestinian Authority officials. Shin Bet’s head then briefed Netanyahu, but urgent talks involving military and intelligence officials produced no action. Abu Zaida then briefed a contact in the UAE presidency, which led to the Gulf nation’s intelligence outfit exchanging notes with Shin Bet. After no visible effects ensued, the Emirati president, Mohammed bin Zayed, was persuaded to directly contact Netanyahu — and is reported to have been surprised by the Israeli PM’s insouciance. Meanwhile, following similar warnings from Cairo, Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, flew to Israel to convey his concerns, advising that the economic stranglehold over Gaza be eased to avert a catastrophe. His efforts, too, went unheeded. Untrue tales of beheaded babies and rape were immediately coughed up. The Israeli media’s take on all this evidence focuses mainly on Netanyahu’s failure to share the information he had received with the defence establishment. His reticence is clearly questionable, but it is at best a side story. Given that many of the warnings were conveyed via Shin Bet, it is ridiculous to pretend that the military/intelligence organs were in the dark. In fact, in the immediate aftermath of Al Aqsa Flood, the Hamas-led operation on Oct 7, 2023, it was already impossible to believe that, given their intrusive surveillance of Gaza, the Israelis were unaware of what was brewing. It soon emerged that reports of unusual activity from the depleted IDF contingents posted on Gaza’s periphery — mostly young soldiers with little experience — were similarly ignored. More experienced troops had been redeployed to the occupied West Bank, to aid Zionist settlers in their acts of extreme violence against Palestinians. Even after he was informed of the Oct 7 ‘surprise’, Netanyahu took his time to react, and it was hours before the IDF sprang into action in the kibbutzim that were attacked. We might never know how many of the Israeli fatalities that day can be accounted for by the IDF’s belated killing spree. But untrue tales of beheaded babies and systematic rape were immediately coughed up to attract international sympathy. The hasbara was rebuffed shortly afterwards, but continues to resurface. The Israeli lie that the Hamas operation was masterminded by Iran never had a leg to stand on, so it gradually made way for other false claims but continues to be resurrected whenever required. In the liberal media across Israel and the West, Oct 7 tends to be seen as a consequence of both the viciousness of Hamas and its allies and the complacency of the Israeli security state, its conviction that Hamas wouldn’t dare try anything worse than lobbing a handful of homemade missiles every now and then. This is nonsense. The far more likely explanation is that the Zionist chieftains actually wanted Hamas to do its worst, since that would give them an excuse to accelerate the Palestinian genocide. That goal was unhesitatingly accomplished. The acclaimed Israeli documentary NAZA, a title that appropriately invokes both the Nazis and Gaza, reportedly highlights the efficiency of mass murder and exposes the banality of evil in the AI era. Consisting of interviews with anonymous Israeli cogs in a genocidal machine, it might help to alert Zionists in Israel and far beyond to the reality of exactly what they have been supporting. However, three years after Israel embarked on the final phase of the Palestinian genocide with Western assistance (epitomised by the absurd Board of Peace), there are no signs of a reversal of fortunes.
articles.author: Mahir Ali

articles.title: Saudi deployment
articles.content: WITH confirmation that members of the Makkah Defence Alliance will be deploying their forces to Saudi Arabia, it appears that the kingdom is preparing for a full-scale war with the pro-Iran Houthi Ansarallah movement. Senior civil and military leaders from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiyemetin Riyadh on Monday to chart a course forward. Though details are sparse, the three defence allies agreed to ensure “rapid deployment in the Kingdom, in accordance with … the national legislation of the parties.” As collective defence is a central pillar of the trilateral alliance, such developments were expected. Members of the MDA also condemned the attacks on Saudi Arabia, particularly alleged attempts to target the holy cities in Hejaz. It is hoped that, from Pakistan’s perspective, these developments only reflect a commitment to defend Saudi Arabia from outside aggression. It would be ill-advised for Pakistan, Turkiye or any other external actor to jump into the Yemeni quagmire. Pakistan has decades-old defence ties to the kingdom, and the pact only reflects a solidification of this relationship. The defence of the holy cities is also a sensitive matter, and Pakistan has in the past contributed troops to protect them. But getting dragged into the Yemeni civil war — which has pit Ansarallah against the Yemeni government, backed by Saudi Arabia — is another story altogether. There was considerable pressure on Pakistan in 2015 from Riyadh to get involved in its operation against the Houthis. Pakistan, thanks to the collective wisdom of parliament, at that time had wisely stayed away from any such undertaking. Similar wisdom is required at this juncture. This country values its deep ties with Saudi Arabia, and should do all it can to protect the kingdom from external aggression. But putting Pakistani boots on the ground in Yemen should be avoided. The fighting in Yemen, both between Ansarallah and the government, as well as between the Houthis and the Saudis, has intensified. At this point chances of a ceasefire seem remote. This conflict has been raging since 2015, and previous external attacks, including by the US and Israel, have failed to dislodge the Houthis. To prevent a fresh humanitarian catastrophe within Yemen, as well as the spread of this conflict across the region, there is an immediate need to end the hostilities. States such as Oman, which has channels open both with the Houthis as well as Saudi Arabia, can perhaps play a mediatory role. The basic requirements of a truce should include an end to all attacks on Saudi Arabia, free passage through Bab al-Mandeb, as well as a halt to all external attacks across Yemen. Only a political process led by Yemenis, and acceptable to all factions in the country, can bring internal peace, as well as guarantee the security of neighbouring states.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Housing policy
articles.content: THE government has finally launched the national housing policy in collaboration with UN Habitat, marking the first update in 25 years. The delay is hard to defend. The housing deficit is estimated at around 13m units and growing. The population keeps rising, cities keep filling up, and socio-economic pressures are splitting families into smaller households. Land and construction cost more every year. Mortgage finance is negligible. Planning is absent or weak. Families shut out of the formal market end up in informal settlements and unapproved housing schemes. The new policy promises affordable housing, easier finance, secure land tenure and the upgrading of informal settlements. These are welcome objectives. Delivery will be the problem. Take the Apna Ghar programme. By Sept 4, banks had approved Rs351.3bn in financing, but only Rs51.13bn had been released. The programme is young, and disbursement may speed up. The country has no shortage of policy papers. It lacks institutions that answer for results, and a clear division of responsibility between the federation, the provinces and development authorities. Housing cannot be treated as a matter of bricks and mortgages alone. Subsidised loans help individual households, but they do nothing for the shortage of affordable land. Cheap credit does not raise incomes or bring down the price of cement and steel. The state must make serviced plots available, extend transport and utilities, enforce zoning laws and allow denser, vertical building. For years private societies have spread over farmland while cities went unplanned and the urban poor were pushed to the margins. The result is sprawl, long commutes and lost cropland. The cabinet has reportedly asked for strict compliance with zoning laws and more vertical construction. That direction should be turned into rules, with penalties for breaking them. The policy should be judged by how many low- and middle-income families actually get homes, not by the value of loans approved or disbursed. Every target needs a deadline and regular progress reports. The housing ministry and the State Bank already review Apna Ghar weekly. The same discipline should extend to the new policy. Land and building rules are provincial subjects, so the provinces must agree to the targets. Without that, the 13m figure will keep climbing.
articles.author: Editorial
